title: Double Dissociation Detective
summary: Read six fictional case files and return a verdict on each: not enough evidence, a severity difference, a single dissociation, a double dissociation, or a crossover the tasks cannot support.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a double dissociation from a single dissociation, a general severity difference and a difference too small to resolve.
Explain why a crossover rules out task difficulty as an explanation, and what it leaves open.
Reference a score to its own control group rather than comparing raw percentages across tasks.
Judge whether a difference is larger than the measurement precision of the test that produced it.
Identify task impurity in a case where a real crossover fails to isolate the process of interest.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native select, range, radio and button controls throughout; the test-length slider announces '55 items per task' rather than a bare number. The interval plot is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table giving raw score, control mean and standard deviation, control-referenced score, its 95% interval and whether each within-person difference is resolvable. Point markers are filled or hollow by shape as well as fill, the table states 'clearly below the control range' in words, and every value is printed beside its marker. Verdicts and case changes are announced through the shell's polite live region. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers so the page never scrolls sideways; the primary chart is pinned so it stays visible while the verdict controls are reached. Heading levels do not skip, reduced motion is honoured, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Single and double dissociations: what a crossover rules out, what measurement precision permits, and where task impurity defeats both
simulationNotes: Six invented case files with invented people, tasks and control groups. Every score is referenced to its own control group as z = (score - control mean) / control SD. Precision is modelled with a binomial standard error, SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/n) divided by the control SD, and a within-person difference counts as resolvable when it exceeds 1.96 times the standard error of the difference. Classification follows the logic rather than the size of the gap: no resolvable difference gives insufficient evidence, one gives a single dissociation, two in the same direction give a general severity difference, two in opposite directions give a double dissociation, and a case flagged as task-impure gives a confounded crossover. Deliberate simplifications: the observed proportion is held fixed while test length varies so the slider isolates precision; control mean and SD are treated as known exactly, whereas proper single-case comparison uses a modified t test and gives wider intervals; and the binomial error assumes independent, equally difficult items. Reference values at the default 40 items per task - case 1 difference 4.75 SD against 2.63 needed, case 2 2.38 and 2.62 against 1.79 and 1.73, case 3 6.52 and 4.07 against 2.43 and 1.78, case 4 0.18 against 2.16, case 5 1.70 and 1.80 against 1.97 and 1.94, case 6 4.47 and 6.07 against 2.14 and 2.83. No real person, published case, clinical instrument or norm is reproduced, and nothing on the page diagnoses, assesses or gives a prognosis for anybody.
